title: DNA Analysis (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand what DNA tests can and cannot tell you, how samples are handled, and how to protect privacy and dignity. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain DNA, genes and the main kinds of tests in plain words.
Read a sample report and say what it does and does not mean.
Weigh benefits and risks of sharing genetic data.
task: Produce a two-page plain-language explainer on DNA testing with a risk list and a consent checklist.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. You will not handle real samples or interpret anyone's results.
standard: Facts are correct and sourced; limits are stated; no diagnosis is offered; privacy risks are named; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Lab assistants, health communicators, teachers, curious adults.
modules: DNA in plain words
Understand
DNA is the code inside almost every cell that carries instructions for how a body is built and runs. You do not need chemistry to understand the main idea.
DNA is made of four letters arranged in a very long order. Genes are sections that carry instructions.
You inherit about half your DNA from each parent, with small changes.
Most traits depend on many genes and on life, such as food, health and environment.
A test reads some parts of DNA, never the whole story of a person.
Height is influenced by hundreds of genes and also by food and health in childhood. Two brothers with the same parents can differ by several centimetres.
Draw a one-page picture: DNA to genes to traits to environment, with plain labels.
Picture is accurate and a non-expert can explain it back.
Kinds of DNA tests
Understand
"A DNA test" can mean very different things, with different uses and limits.
Ancestry tests estimate where your ancestors may have lived, using comparison groups.
Health-risk tests report chances of some conditions; carrier tests show if you could pass a condition on.
Paternity and relationship tests compare DNA between people; forensic tests compare crime-scene samples.
Medical diagnosis belongs with a clinician and an accredited lab.

A carrier test reports that a couple each carry a change linked to a blood condition. This does not mean any child will be affected; it means that, for a typical recessive condition, the chance is about one in four per pregnancy, and a genetic counsellor explains the options.
Build a table of five test kinds with purpose, what it cannot tell you, and who should explain results.
Each row states a limit and a right person to explain.
From sample to result
Analyse
Mistakes can enter at every step. Quality systems exist to catch them.
Steps: consent, collect, label, store, extract, read, check, report.
Chain of custody records who held the sample and when.
Errors: mislabelling, contamination, poor storage, misreading.
Good labs use barcodes, two-person checks and repeat tests.
Two tubes are swapped at the front desk. A barcode scan at the lab finds a mismatch with the form and stops the run, avoiding a wrong report.
Map the sample steps and write one quality check for each step.
Every step has a check and an owner.
Reading a result safely
Analyse
Numbers like "twice the risk" sound alarming but need context.
Relative risk compares groups; absolute risk is the real chance for a person.
Gene changes whose meaning is unclear are common and are not proof of disease.
Results can be wrong or incomplete; confirm important findings in an accredited lab.
Only a genetic counsellor or clinician explains health results.
A report says a 50% higher chance of a condition. The absolute chance changes from 2 in 100 to 3 in 100. A counsellor explains that lifestyle and screening matter more than fear.
Explain a sample result (given by your mentor) to a peer in under two minutes using absolute numbers.
Peer repeats the meaning correctly and does not panic.
Marketing and overclaims
Evaluate
Some adverts promise a perfect diet, talent or career from your DNA. Most go beyond evidence.
Look for independent studies, regulator approval and clear limits.
Be wary of "personalised diet" or "talent" claims and of high prices.
Check whether samples are analysed in an accredited lab.
Read the privacy terms before sending a sample.
An advert promises a diet plan from a saliva test with no study cited. The learner marks it "unproven" and notes the missing evidence.
Review two real adverts with a five-point checklist.
Each advert has a scored list with reasons.
Privacy and family impact
Evaluate
Your DNA also describes your relatives. Sharing it can affect them.
Data may be sold, hacked, or requested by authorities or insurers in some places.
Findings can reveal unexpected relatives or risks for the family.
Consent must be informed and free, with the right to withdraw.
Never test a child or another adult without proper consent and guidance.
A family agrees before testing that surprises will be shared only with a counsellor present. Two siblings opt out of learning some results.
Write a consent checklist with at least eight questions.
Each question is clear and answerable yes or no.
Ethics, fairness and access
Evaluate
Genetic science can help or harm depending on how it is used.
No test should be forced on employees, students or insurance applicants.
Some groups have less data in reference sets, so results can be less accurate for them.
Respect cultural and faith views.
Ask who benefits, who pays and who is left out.
A research project adds samples from under-represented communities with community agreement, improving accuracy for them.
Discuss two cases with peers and write a reasoned view on each.
Peers reach a view with at least two reasons and one risk.
Write a plain-language explainer
Create
Bring everything into a two-page guide that a curious non-expert can use.
Use short sentences and a glossary.
Include the limits, privacy risks and who to ask for help.
Test with one person aged under 25 and one over 55.
Date the guide and plan a yearly review.
A reader says, "Now I know to ask a counsellor, not a website, about my result."
Finish and test the explainer.
Both readers can list three limits of DNA tests.
quiz: What is DNA?
The instruction code in cells. (Covered in module 1: DNA in plain words. To pass that module: Picture is accurate and a non-expert can explain it back.)
Is a result destiny?
No; it is a chance. (Covered in module 4: Reading a result safely. To pass that module: Peer repeats the meaning correctly and does not panic.)
Name two test kinds.
Ancestry and carrier (or health risk, paternity). (Covered in module 2: Kinds of DNA tests. To pass that module: Each row states a limit and a right person to explain.)
Why chain of custody?
To show who held the sample. (Covered in module 3: From sample to result. To pass that module: Every step has a check and an owner.)
Who explains health results?
A genetic counsellor or clinician. (Covered in module 4: Reading a result safely. To pass that module: Peer repeats the meaning correctly and does not panic.)
Name one marketing red flag.
A big promise with no evidence. (Covered in module 5: Marketing and overclaims. To pass that module: Each advert has a scored list with reasons.)
Why does DNA affect relatives?
Relatives share genes. (Covered in module 6: Privacy and family impact. To pass that module: Each question is clear and answerable yes or no.)
Name a data risk.
Sale, hacking or misuse by insurers. (Covered in module 6: Privacy and family impact. To pass that module: Each question is clear and answerable yes or no.)
Can employers force tests?
They should not. (Covered in module 7: Ethics, fairness and access. To pass that module: Peers reach a view with at least two reasons and one risk.)
Why is diverse data needed?
Results are less accurate for under-represented groups. (Covered in module 7: Ethics, fairness and access. To pass that module: Peers reach a view with at least two reasons and one risk.)
rubric: Clear and tested with a reader
Claims such as 'proves' with no limit
Each claim says what the test can and cannot show
Each claim carries its error rate or confidence range from a public source
Consent covers storage, sharing and deletion
Consent tested on a reader who restated it in their own words, with the local genetic-data rule noted

local: Genetic testing and data laws differ by place; some tests need a clinician.
